extracted.intended_audience: International Searching and Preliminary Examining Authorities, patent examiners, and patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for international search and preliminary examination under the PCT, covering how to treat disclosures (including Internet), how to assess dates, novelty and inventive step, and related procedural evidentiary rules. Intended to direct examiners in selecting/citing prior art and forming written opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No notification when same priority date applications from different applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: No notification should be given where two applications (international or otherwise) of the same priority date and relating to the same invention are received from two different applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select later documents relevant to understanding the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents published on or after the international filing date may nevertheless be relevant (for example, a later document containing the principle or theory underlying the invention or showing that the reasoning or facts underlying the invention are incorrect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The international search is not extended for this purpose, but documents of this nature known to the search examiner may be selected for citation in the international search report and their relevance explained in the written opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a disclosure is regarded as made available to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is regarded as made available to the public if, at the relevant date, it was possible for members of the public to gain knowledge from the content and there was no bar of confidentiality restricting use or dissemination of that knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the disclosure only provides the month or year, the content is presumed to have been made available on the last day of that month or year respectively, unless evidence proves otherwise (see paragraphs 11.02–11.05).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet disclosures treated like other disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosure on the Internet or on an on-line database is considered in the same manner as other forms of disclosure; information first disclosed on the Internet is considered publicly available as of the date the disclosure was publicly posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems may arise in establishing the date of publication and whether the disclosure has been modified over time (see further guidance on trusted vs unknown websites and technical means to establish dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish disclosures on trusted publisher web sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures made on web sites of trusted publishers (e.g. on-line scientific journals, web sites of newspapers, periodicals, TV/radio stations) give the publication date which, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, should be taken at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should cite such Internet disclosures in the international search report and use them in the written opinion and preliminary examination accordingly. The onus is on the applicant to prove otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: When publication date is insufficiently identified
rubrics_metrics.description: If the publication date is not sufficiently identified to establish whether it is prior to the relevant date (for example only month/year given equal to priority month/year), the Authority may need to make enquiries with the owner of the web site to establish the publication date to sufficient accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of web sites of unknown reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: For Internet disclosures from web sites of unknown reliability (private individuals, clubs, commercial advertising sites, etc.), where no explicit publication date is given, the Authority may consider using technical means available to it to attempt to reveal the publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See list of technical means (paragraph 11.17) and procedures for print-out and citation (paragraph 11.18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical means to establish Internet publication dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical means include: (a) date information embedded in the Internet disclosure itself (hidden in programming), (b) indexing dates given by search engines (usually later than actual publication), and (c) information from Internet archiving databases (e.g. Internet Archive Wayback Machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an electronic document establishing the publication date is obtained, make a print-out mentioning both the URL and the date and cite it in the international search report as an “L” document; cite the relevant Internet disclosure according to content relevance and the established date. If unable to establish the date and the disclosure affects novelty/inventive step, cite it as “L” and give the print-out date as publication date (see paragraph 16.75(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust internet-given publication date when reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an Internet disclosure explicitly mentions a publication date and that date is not contradicted by available information and is accurate enough to establish relevance under Rule 33.1(a) and Rule 64.1(b), the examiner should trust the date given and use it in the search report and preliminary examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The onus is on the applicant to prove otherwise. Note indexing dates are normally later than actual publication and do not necessarily contradict an internal date given by the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume internet content unchanged absent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of evidence to the contrary, the examiner should assume that the content of the Internet disclosure has not changed over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in citation practice for patent vs non-patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, no non-patent document is cited in the international search report if its publication/public availability date is clearly the same as, or later than, the filing date of the international application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, patent documents published on or after the filing date are cited if their filing or priority date is earlier than the filing date of the searched application; such published patent documents are cited in the search report but are not considered prior art for Article 33(2) and (3) and are mentioned in the preliminary examination report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing documents reproducing an earlier disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a document (including video, audio, multimedia retrieved from the Internet) reproduces an oral disclosure or a disclosure from a prior use or sale that was publicly available before the relevant date, that document should be cited with the date that the earlier disclosure was first made publicly available indicated as the date of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an Internet publication of an earlier disclosure, content is considered publicly available as of the earlier disclosure date if this can be established (e.g. date recorded, written reference). If an earlier disclosure date cannot be established, treat it as publicly available as of the date it was posted on the Internet. The written opinion and preliminary examination report should call attention to such non-written disclosure (Rule 70.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to remove doubt when difficulty establishing date
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is difficulty establishing whether the date of publication/public availability of a document is the same as, or later than, the filing date, the International Searching Authority should try to remove any doubt that may exist and may cite additional documents providing evidence in case of doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any indication in a document of the date of its publication should be accepted as correct unless proof to the contrary is offered. If the applicant presents sound reasons for doubting that the document is prior art and further investigation does not remove doubt, the examiner should not pursue the matter further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant date may differ between claims or parts of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant date for prior art purposes is the international filing date or, where there is a valid claim to priority, that priority date. Different claims or different alternatives in one claim may have different relevant dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of novelty and inventive step must be considered against each claim (or part of a claim where alternatives are specified) and prior art for one claim may not be citable against another claim with an earlier relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty — definition (lack of novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: For international preliminary examination, the invention, as defined by a claim, lacks novelty if every element or step is explicitly or inherently disclosed within the prior art defined in Rule 64.1, including any features implicit to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency requires extrinsic evidence showing the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present. Inherency may not be established by probabilities or possibilities. Well-known equivalents not disclosed in a prior art document are not considered when assessing novelty (they are a matter for inventive step). The same considerations apply when producing a written opinion and in selecting documents for the international search report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art disclosure must be enabling to defeat novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the claimed invention; a document that is not enabling for the claimed invention does not necessarily defeat novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinarily enablement may be inferred for patent documents. For non-patent literature that raises questions as to enablement, the examiner should determine that the prior art would have enabled a person skilled in the art. Knowledge from outside the prior art document may be considered where appropriate (see appendix to Chapter 12). A prior art document not enabling for novelty may still be relied on for inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for assessing novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: For assessment of novelty the examiner should: (i) evaluate the elements of the claimed invention; (ii) determine if a document forms part of the 'prior art'; (iii) assess whether each and every element or step was explicitly or inherently disclosed in combination by the document to a person skilled in the art on the date of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent or implicit disclosure standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of novelty may arise from explicit disclosure or from an inherent/implicit teaching of a document where, in carrying out the teaching of the prior document, the skilled person would inevitably arrive at a result falling within the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherent lack of novelty should be raised by the examiner only where there can be no reasonable doubt as to the practical effect of the prior teaching; otherwise it should be considered under inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation for novelty (purpose/use statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting claims for novelty, statements reciting the purpose or intended use must be evaluated to determine whether the recited purpose/use results in a structural difference (or, for process claims, a difference in steps) between the claimed invention and the prior art. Non-distinctive characteristics of a particular intended use should be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a substance claimed for use as a catalyst is not novel over the same substance known as a dye unless the use implies a distinguishing form (e.g. additives). A 'mould for molten steel' implies limitations that distinguish it from a plastic ice cube tray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining documents not permitted for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering novelty it is not permissible to combine separate items of prior art together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if a primary document explicitly refers to a second document, the teachings of the second may be regarded as incorporated to the extent indicated. It is permissible to use dictionaries to interpret terms and to rely on additional documents as evidence to show sufficiency or inherency of the primary disclosure (see paragraph 12.02 and appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives disclosed in prior art anticipate Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim contains alternatives (e.g. Markush claim), any alternatives disclosed in the prior art are anticipated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs specific disclosures for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific example in prior art that falls within a claimed generic parameter anticipates the generic claim. Conversely, a genus does not always anticipate a species unless the specific example is identified with sufficient specificity in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art identifies the claimed example with sufficient specificity, that example lacks novelty regardless of other species described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranges: specific examples and selection inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific example in prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range. Where prior art discloses a range that touches/overlaps the claimed range but not a specific example within it, novelty must be decided case-by-case; narrow claimed ranges may be selection inventions if not sufficiently disclosed and if unexpected results support them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected results may also render claims unobvious (inventive step).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent practices on extrinsic knowledge for novelty (A12.02[1])
rubrics_metrics.description: One practice: the prior document must provide a sufficient disclosure on its effective date (publication date) together with knowledge generally available on that effective date to supply every element/step of the claimed invention to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities following this practice do not consider knowledge made available after the prior document's publication date when assessing whether it disclosed the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent practices on extrinsic knowledge for novelty (A12.02[2])
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative practice: the prior document must provide a sufficient disclosure on the 'relevant date' of the claim being searched or examined; Authorities following this practice consider knowledge that became available after the publication date but before the relevant date when determining sufficiency of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities differ; those not following these guidelines may still rely on the prior art document for inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step — definition (non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the prior art, it is not, at the relevant date, obvious to a person skilled in the art. Novelty and inventive step are different criteria: inventive step assesses whether the invention as a whole would not have been obvious to the skilled person in light of the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple items of prior art may be combined in determining inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art scope for inventive step (Article 33(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'prior art' for inventive step is as defined in Article 33(3); it does not include later published applications or patents, although in certain circumstances later published applications/patents may be cited in the international preliminary examination report (see paragraph 11.07 and 16.73).

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as 'obvious' for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is whether, at the relevant date, it would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art to arrive at something within the claim having regard to the art known at that time. 'Obvious' denotes what follows plainly or logically from the prior art without exercise of skill beyond that expected of the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic considerations: (i) consider the claimed invention as a whole; (ii) consider references as a whole and whether the skilled person would be motivated to combine teachings with a reasonable expectation of success; (iii) avoid impermissible hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use later knowledge when assessing inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering inventive step (distinct from novelty), it is fair to construe any published document in the light of subsequent knowledge and to have regard to all knowledge generally available to the person skilled in the art at the relevant date of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing combinations and invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining inventive step the invention must be considered as a whole; it is not sufficient to argue that separate features of a combination are known or obvious individually, unless there is no functional relationship (mere juxtaposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim should be directed to technical features. Various ways a skilled person may arrive at an invention should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for applicant acknowledgements and general knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: When identifying the contribution of the invention against the art, account should be taken of what the applicant acknowledges to be known; such acknowledgements should generally be regarded as correct unless amended. Also consider further prior art and the general knowledge of the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art used must be enabling for what it teaches; any combination of items of prior art and general knowledge relied upon must provide enablement with respect to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment steps for inventive step (13.08)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following considerations should be applied: (i) determine scope of claimed invention; (ii) determine scope of relevant prior art; (iii) determine the person skilled in the art; (iv) identify differences and similarities between prior art and claimed invention; (v) assess whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to the skilled person given the prior art and general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation, reasonable likelihood of success, and problem-solution approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention is obvious if prior art or general knowledge would have motivated the skilled person, with reasonable likelihood of success, to reach the claimed invention by substituting, combining or modifying prior art. One particular way to determine inventive step is the problem-solution approach (see appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The person skilled in the art is a hypothetical person of ordinary skill, aware of common general knowledge at the relevant date, with access to everything in the prior art and the normal means/capacity for routine experimentation. If the problem prompts seeking solution in another field, the skilled person in that field is relevant; sometimes a group may be the appropriate skilled 'person'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible combination of teachings for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to combine teachings of two or more prior art references for inventive step only where such combination would be obvious to the person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining obviousness of combination consider: (i) whether nature/content of documents makes combination likely; (ii) whether documents are from similar or neighboring technical fields or reasonably pertinent to the problem. Motivation need not be the same as the applicant’s; prior art may suggest combination for a different purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions under which combining prior art leads to lack of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Combination, substitution or modification of teachings leads to lack of inventive step only where the skilled person would have been motivated by the prior art or general knowledge with a reasonable likelihood to combine/modify and achieve the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining parts of the same document is obvious if reasonable basis exists to associate them. It is generally obvious to combine a well-known textbook/dictionary with other prior art. Some instances can lead to lack of inventive step from a single item of prior art (see appendix and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of obviousness (illustrative guides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where claimed invention should be regarded as obvious include: (a) application of known measures in an obvious way such that at least one way of supplying missing claim features would naturally occur to the skilled person; (b) differences that are merely use of well-known equivalents; (c) a new use of a well-known material employing known properties; (d) substitution of a recently developed material whose properties make it plainly suitable for that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are guides only; the applicable principle is always 'was it obvious to a person skilled in the art?' Examiners should avoid forcing a case into an example that does not clearly apply.
